title: What is the difference between margin and markup, and why do candidates mix them up?
description: Margin versus markup explained with worked examples, how to convert between them, and why mixing them up changes a case answer.
hook: Margin is profit divided by the selling price; markup is the same profit divided by the cost. Candidates mix them up because both describe "profit as a percentage" of the same sale, and under pressure it is easy to forget which denominator you are using. The gap between the two is large enough to change a case answer.
body:
The definitions

  • Margin = profit ÷ price.
  • Markup = profit ÷ cost.

A product costs $80 and sells for $100, so profit is $20. Margin is $20 ÷ $100 = 20%. Markup is $20 ÷ $80 = 25%. Same sale, same $20, two different percentages.

Because cost is always smaller than price (when the product is profitable), the markup is always the bigger number. If you calculate a markup below the margin, you have swapped the denominators. The glossary entry has a one-line version to memorise.

Why candidates mix them up

Three reasons. Both are quoted as "a percentage on the product", so they sound interchangeable. Different people use different conventions: retailers and restaurants often talk about markup on cost, while finance teams and annual reports talk about margins on revenue. And in a case, the interviewer may just say "they make 30%" without saying which.

Converting between them

  • Markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin). A 20% margin is 0.2 ÷ 0.8 = 25% markup.
  • Margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup). A 50% markup is 0.5 ÷ 1.5 = 33.3% margin.

If you forget the formulas, pick a cost of $100 and work it out: a 50% markup makes the price $150, so the margin is $50 ÷ $150 = 33.3%.

Markup on costMargin on price
25%20%
33.3%25%
50%33.3%
100%50%
150%60%

Why it matters in a case

Sizing profit

A client says it "adds 50% to cost". If you treat that as a 50% margin, you overstate profit by half. On $1M of sales, a 50% markup is a 33.3% margin, so profit is about $333k, not $500k.

Setting a price

A client wants a 30% gross margin on an item that costs $70. A 30% margin means cost must be 70% of the price, so the price is $70 ÷ 0.70 = $100. Adding a 30% markup instead gives $70 × 1.3 = $91, and a margin of only $21 ÷ $91 = 23%. The candidate who confuses the two underprices the product by $9 a unit.

Strong: "To earn a 30% gross margin on a $70 cost, the price has to be $100, because cost must be 70% of price. I'd then check whether customers will pay $100, and whether delivery or returns costs change the target."
Weak: "30% on $70 is $21, so price it at $91."

Following a product through the supply chain

Markups multiply as a product moves from maker to shelf. A manufacturer's cost is $40. A wholesaler buys it and applies a 25% markup, selling at $50. A retailer buys at $50 and applies a 100% markup, selling at $100. The retailer's margin is $50 ÷ $100 = 50%. The shelf price is 2.5 times the manufacturer's cost, a combined markup of 150%, not 25% + 100% = 125%. In a channel or distribution case, work through each step in dollars rather than adding percentages.

Check which costs are included

Margin also depends on what counts as cost. A $20 profit on an $80 purchase price is a gross margin. Once you take off delivery, card fees and returns, the contribution margin is lower, and after rent and staff the operating margin is lower still. Never present a gross margin as if it were net profitability. The 20 formulas explained sets out the difference between gross, contribution and operating margins.

A habit to build

Whenever you hear a profit percentage, ask: "Is that on price or on cost?" It takes three seconds. When you give one yourself, say the denominator out loud: "a 20% margin on revenue".

Practice

1. A retailer buys a lamp for $60 and sells it for $90. What are the margin and markup?

Show the answer

Profit is $30. Margin: $30 ÷ $90 = 33.3%. Markup: $30 ÷ $60 = 50%.

2. An item costs $45. What price gives a 40% margin?

Show the answer

Cost must be 60% of price, so price = $45 ÷ 0.6 = $75. Check: $30 profit ÷ $75 = 40%.

3. A wholesaler applies a 25% markup and has $5M of sales. What is its gross profit?

Show the answer

A 25% markup is a 20% margin, so gross profit is 20% × $5M = $1M. Treating 25% as the margin would give $1.25M, overstating profit by a quarter.
